claim.pdf_says: FUNCTION CONVERT ( argument-1 source-format destination-format )  — BOTH 'FUNCTION' and 'CONVERT' carry an underline in the printed general format (verified by rendering page 859 at 300 dpi and cropping the line: two separate underline rules sit beneath FUNCTION and beneath CONVERT).
claim.markdown_says: <u>FUNCTION</u> CONVERT ( argument-1 source-format destination-format )   (ISO_COBOL.md line 34553 — only FUNCTION is wrapped in <u>…</u>; CONVERT is left plain)
claim.why_it_matters: Per 5.2.6.2 an underlined word is a REQUIRED word and a non-underlined word is an OPTIONAL word that may be omitted without changing the meaning. Marking FUNCTION underlined but CONVERT not asserts a positive (and false) distinction: it reads as though 'FUNCTION ( argument-1 … )' were legal. Every sibling function in clause 15 uses the '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>NAME</u>' form (ABS, ANNUITY, ATAN, COMBINED-DATETIME, CONCAT, CURRENT-DATE, …), so CONVERT is the outlier. The identical defect exists at line 38293 for TEST-NUMVAL.

verdict.reasoning:
Independently confirmed at the pixel level, not merely by visual impression. Rendered page 859 at 300 dpi (E:/Temp/specrecon/v859/spec_p859.png). On the 15.19.2 General format line, a scan for horizontal dark runs finds exactly one underline row, y=1524, containing TWO separate rules: x=342-541 and x=567-749, with a 26 px gap between them. Computing the glyph-band (y=1470-1515, which excludes the underline row) column extents for that same line yields word boxes: FUNCTION (340-543), CONVERT (565-751), '(' (770-782), 'argument-1' (795-1014), 'source-format destination-format )' (1030-1691). The two underline rules align to within 2 px of the FUNCTION and CONVERT word boxes respectively, and NO rule exists under any operand. So the printed standard underlines both FUNCTION and CONVERT, and nothing else on the line. The claim's PDF quotation is exact.

The markdown quotation is also exact: line 34553 of specs/ISO_COBOL.md reads verbatim '<u>FUNCTION</u> CONVERT ( argument-1 source-format destination-format )'. CONVERT carries no <u> markup.

I checked the alternative explanations and all fail. (a) Not a lost-formatting artifact of a fence-based transcription style: this line is NOT inside a code fence — it is an inline line using HTML <u> markup, the same family as 16 sibling general formats that DO mark both words ('<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>ABS</u>', '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>ANNUITY</u>', '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>ATAN</u>', '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>COMBINED-DATETIME</u>', '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>CONCAT</u>', '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>CURRENT-DATE</u>', etc.). A regex over the whole file shows the underline-marked family has exactly 18 members: 16 of the form '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>NAME</u>' and precisely 2 of the form '<u>FUNCTION</u> NAME' — CONVERT (34553) and TEST-NUMVAL (38293). (There is a separate, larger set of function general formats transcribed inside ``` fences with no underline markup at all, e.g. 'FUNCTION ACOS ( argument-1 )' at line 34065; those are uniformly unmarked and are a different transcription style, not a counterexample to this asymmetry.) (b) Not reflow, page-break furniture, hyphenation, or wrapping — the whole format is on one line in both sources. (c) It does change meaning: an asymmetric marking on a single line is an affirmative assertion, not a neutral omission. Under 5.2.2 (keywords are 'shown in uppercase and underlined in general formats … required in order to select the functionality') and 5.2.3 (optional words are 'shown in uppercase and not underlined … may be written to add clarity'), the markdown as written classifies CONVERT as an optional word, which would make 'FUNCTION ( argument-1 source-format destination-format )' a legal reference to the CONVERT function. That is false and is a real semantic corruption for any consumer that derives keyword-required-ness from the underline markup.

I also verified the claim's second instance rather than accepting it: line 38293 sits on printed page 956, which I rendered at 300 dpi. The underline scan finds one rule row (y=1021) with two separate runs, and the crop shows plainly that both FUNCTION and TEST-NUMVAL are underlined in the printed standard while '( argument-1 )' is not. The markdown leaves TEST-NUMVAL plain. That instance is confirmed too.

The only inaccuracy in the claim is its supporting citation: it attributes the underline rule to '5.2.6.2', but in this document 5.2.6.2 is 'Brackets'. The governing clauses are 5.2.2 (Keywords) and 5.2.3 (Optional words). The substance of the rationale is unaffected.
verdict.corrected_description: CONFIRMED, with one citation correction. On printed page 859, clause 15.19.2 General format, the standard prints two underline rules — one spanning FUNCTION (x 342-541) and one spanning CONVERT (x 567-749) — pixel-aligned to those two word boxes, with no rule under the operands. specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 34553 renders this as '<u>FUNCTION</u> CONVERT ( argument-1 source-format destination-format )', dropping the underline on CONVERT only. Because the line does mark FUNCTION, the omission is not a neutral loss of formatting but an affirmative miscategorization: under 5.2.2/5.2.3 (NOT 5.2.6.2, which is 'Brackets' — the claim's citation is wrong) an unmarked uppercase word in a general format is an optional word, so the transcription implies 'FUNCTION ( argument-1 … )' is a legal CONVERT reference. Within the file's inline underline-marked family of function general formats (18 lines), 16 correctly use '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>NAME</u>' and only CONVERT (34553) and TEST-NUMVAL (38293) are defective; the second instance was independently verified against printed page 956, where both FUNCTION and TEST-NUMVAL are underlined. Fix: wrap both function names in <u>…</u>. Note that a larger set of clause-15 general formats is transcribed inside code fences with no underline markup at all (e.g. 'FUNCTION ACOS ( argument-1 )' at line 34065); that is a separate, uniform transcription-style gap, not part of this defect.
